cards.front: How does growth hormone act, and why do its growth effects depend on IGF-1?
cards.back: GH binds a JAK-STAT-linked cytokine-type receptor on most cells, which alters gene transcription. Its growth-promoting and nitrogen-retaining effects are mostly indirect, carried by IGF-1 (somatomedin), made mainly in the liver. GH itself promotes lipolysis and gluconeogenesis and reduces glucose uptake, so it raises blood glucose.

cards.front: List the main therapeutic uses of somatropin (recombinant GH).
cards.back: GH deficiency in children (pituitary dwarfism), Turner syndrome (with timed oestrogen and androgen), growth failure from chronic renal insufficiency in children, adult GH deficiency and AIDS-related wasting. Use in idiopathic short stature is debated, and its use by athletes is banned.

cards.front: What adverse effects limit somatropin therapy?
cards.back: Injection-site pain and lipodystrophy, glucose intolerance, hypothyroidism (by unmasking central TSH deficiency), salt and water retention, myalgia, hand stiffness and headache. Intracranial pressure can rise in a few patients. Immunogenicity is low, so allergy and resistance are uncommon.

cards.front: Why is native somatostatin unsuitable as a drug for acromegaly?
cards.back: Its half-life is only 2 to 3 minutes. It is not selective: it also suppresses insulin, glucagon, TSH, gastrin and gut secretions. Stopping it causes GH rebound. Long-acting analogues (octreotide, lanreotide) are used instead.

cards.front: How does octreotide differ from somatostatin, and what are its uses?
cards.back: A synthetic octapeptide about 40 times more potent than somatostatin at suppressing GH, with a half-life of about 90 minutes. It is only a weak inhibitor of insulin. Uses: acromegaly, secretory diarrhoea (carcinoid, AIDS, chemotherapy or diabetes related) and IV control of variceal bleeding. Adverse effects: gallstones, steatorrhoea and abdominal pain.

cards.front: How does pegvisomant work, and when is it used?
cards.back: It is a pegylated mutant GH. One of its two receptor-binding sites binds more tightly and the other more weakly than native GH, so it allows receptor dimerisation but blocks the conformational change needed for signalling: a GH receptor antagonist. Pegylation slows clearance. Daily s.c. treatment normalises IGF-1 in most patients with acromegaly. It does not reduce GH secretion (GH levels may rise), so response is followed by IGF-1. KDT lists it for acromegaly due to small adenomas; it is used when GH excess persists after surgery.

cards.front: What controls prolactin secretion, and which drugs raise prolactin levels?
cards.back: Dopamine (prolactin-inhibiting factor) keeps prolactin low by acting on D2 receptors of lactotrope cells. Dopamine blockers (chlorpromazine, haloperidol, metoclopramide) and the dopamine-depleting drug reserpine raise prolactin. Suckling keeps levels high after delivery, and prolactinomas are a common cause of hyperprolactinaemia.

cards.text: Cabergoline is the {{first-choice}} agent, given {{twice weekly}}; {{bromocriptine}} is the older ergot-derived drug that has largely been replaced.

cards.front: Classify: gonadotropin preparations
cards.text: Urinary menotropins contain {{FSH plus LH}}; urofollitropin is {{pure FSH}}; {{hCG}} acts at the LH receptor with an action indistinguishable from {{LH}}.

cards.front: Classify: GnRH analogues
cards.text: Agonists: {{goserelin}}, {{leuprolide}}, {{nafarelin}}, {{triptorelin}}. Injectable peptide antagonists: {{ganirelix}}, {{cetrorelix}}, {{degarelix}}, {{abarelix}}. Oral non-peptide antagonists for endometriosis and fibroid symptoms: {{elagolix}}, {{relugolix}}, {{linzagolix}}.

cards.front: Outline the steps in thyroid hormone synthesis and where TSH acts.
cards.back: Iodide is trapped by the Na+/iodide symporter, a step TSH increases. Thyroid peroxidase oxidises it (using H2O2) and attaches it to tyrosyl residues of thyroglobulin as MIT and DIT. Coupling of two DIT gives T4; MIT plus DIT gives T3. Stored colloid is re-endocytosed and proteolysed, releasing T4 and T3; MIT and DIT are deiodinated and the iodide reused. TSH stimulates trapping, organification, coupling and release.

cards.front: Why is T4 called a prohormone of T3?
cards.back: T4 is secreted in larger amounts and is bound much more tightly to plasma proteins, so it acts as a circulating reserve. About a third of T4 is converted to T3 by deiodinases in the liver, kidney and target tissues. T3 is the active form: it binds the nuclear receptor more strongly, acts faster and is about five times more potent.

cards.front: Which deiodinase is inhibited by propylthiouracil, and which antiarrhythmic inhibits both D1 and D2?
cards.back: Propylthiouracil inhibits type 1 deiodinase (D1), found mainly in liver, kidney and thyroid, but not D2. Amiodarone inhibits both D1 and D2. Carbimazole does not. High-dose propranolol and glucocorticoids also reduce T4 to T3 conversion, except in brain and pituitary.

cards.front: How do thyroid hormones increase heart rate and contractility?
cards.back: They act directly on the heart by increasing the myosin isoform with higher Ca2+-ATPase activity. They also raise beta-adrenergic receptor numbers and coupling, so catecholamines have a greater effect. The result is tachycardia, a bounding pulse, higher systolic pressure and atrial fibrillation. Thyroid hormones can also precipitate heart failure or angina.

cards.front: Why is levothyroxine preferred over liothyronine?
cards.back: Liothyronine (T3) acts faster, but its action is short and it carries a higher risk of arrhythmia and angina. Levothyroxine gives a more sustained and uniform effect, and its oral bioavailability is about 75 percent. Liothyronine is not freely available in India and is used IV with T4 only in selected cases such as myxoedema coma.

cards.front: How is myxoedema coma treated?
cards.back: A medical emergency, best managed in intensive care, as intubation and ventilation may be needed. Give everything IV because absorption by other routes is poor. Drug of choice is an IV loading dose of levothyroxine (Katzung: 300 to 400 µg; KDT: 200 to 500 µg), then 50 to 100 µg IV daily until oral therapy is possible. IV T3 can be added, but it is more cardiotoxic; use lower doses in older or cardiac patients. Give IV hydrocortisone if adrenal or pituitary insufficiency may coexist, give IV fluids cautiously (risk of water intoxication), and treat the precipitating infection or heart failure.

cards.front: Which drugs reduce levothyroxine absorption, and which speed its clearance?
cards.back: Absorption is reduced by sucralfate, iron, calcium and proton pump inhibitors, and by food, so levothyroxine is taken on an empty stomach. Enzyme inducers (rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine) speed T4 metabolism and may need a higher dose. Severe hypothyroidism itself reduces absorption.

cards.front: When is subclinical hypothyroidism treated with thyroxine?
cards.back: Subclinical hypothyroidism means raised TSH with normal thyroid hormone levels. Treatment is individualised. Levothyroxine is generally advised when TSH is above 10 mU/L. For milder TSH elevations, close TSH monitoring is appropriate; KDT adds that treatment for TSH 6 to 10 mU/L is optional and preferable if cardiovascular risk factors are present.

cards.front: Name drugs that cause hypothyroidism or goitre, and the mechanism of each.
cards.back: Lithium inhibits hormone release. Amiodarone blocks peripheral T4 to T3 conversion and interferes with hormone action. Sulfonamides and para-aminosalicylic acid impair iodination and coupling. Phenobarbitone, phenytoin, carbamazepine and rifampicin speed T4 breakdown. Iodides and radioiodine can also cause hypothyroidism.

cards.front: What is the pathogenesis of Graves' disease, and why is TSH low in it?
cards.back: An IgG thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin binds the TSH receptor and drives long-lasting thyroid stimulation. The excess hormone suppresses TSH through negative feedback. Stimulation of TSH receptors in periorbital tissue appears to cause exophthalmos. Toxic nodular goitre is TSH-independent, is more common in older people and usually lacks eye signs.

Overdose causes goitre and hypothyroidism, which reverse on stopping
Methimazole (or carbimazole) is about 10 times more potent than propylthiouracil and is the drug of choice
Propylthiouracil is reserved for the first trimester of pregnancy, thyroid storm and intolerance of methimazole (other than agranulocytosis or hepatitis)

Titrate the dose to maternal thyroid status throughout pregnancy

Gamma emission is used for tracing and scanning

Many clinics reserve it for patients over about 25 to 30 years and when surgery is risky (heart failure, angina)
Outpatient, simple and inexpensive

cards.front: Classify: iodine and iodides as thyroid inhibitors
cards.text: Iodine and iodides are the {{fastest-acting}} thyroid inhibitors; their main effect is {{blocking hormone release}}. Excess iodide causes a brief {{Wolff-Chaikoff}} block, and the gland usually {{escapes}} it after a few days.

cards.front: Classify: ionic inhibitors of iodide trapping
cards.text: {{Perchlorate}} is about {{10 times}} more potent than {{thiocyanate}} at blocking the Na+/iodide symporter; both are toxic and not used clinically.

cards.front: Classify: how each thyroid-lowering drug acts
cards.text: Thioamides inhibit {{thyroid peroxidase}}; iodide inhibits {{hormone release}}; propranolol treats {{adrenergic}} symptoms and at high dose reduces {{T4 to T3 conversion}}; radioiodine destroys follicles with {{beta particles}}.

cards.front: Classify: thyroid hormone transport in plasma
cards.text: Thyroid hormones are bound to {{TBG}} (highest affinity), then {{transthyretin}}, then {{albumin}}; only about {{0.03 to 0.08 percent}} of T4 circulates free.

cards.front: How do type 1 and type 2 diabetes differ in cause and insulin levels?
cards.back: Type 1 results from loss of beta cells, usually autoimmune, so circulating insulin is low or absent and ketosis is common. Type 2 involves insulin resistance with impaired beta-cell secretion; insulin levels are normal or high and genetic predisposition is strong. Type 2 accounts for over 90 percent of cases.

cards.front: How does glucose trigger insulin release from beta cells?
cards.back: Glucose is phosphorylated by glucokinase and metabolised, which raises ATP. ATP closes ATP-sensitive K+ channels, depolarising the cell. Calcium enters and insulin granules undergo exocytosis. Oral glucose gives a stronger response than IV glucose because gut incretins (GLP-1, GIP) amplify secretion.

cards.front: What is the mechanism of metformin's glucose-lowering effect?
cards.back: Metformin does not stimulate insulin release, but it needs insulin to act. Its main effect is suppression of hepatic gluconeogenesis and glucose output, through AMPK activation that follows changes in cellular energy status. It also improves insulin-mediated glucose uptake in muscle and fat, and slightly reduces intestinal glucose absorption.

cards.front: How do sulfonylureas lower blood glucose, and why is hypoglycaemia their main risk?
cards.back: They bind the SUR1 subunit of the beta-cell KATP channel and close it. Depolarisation and calcium influx increase insulin release, mainly the second phase, and this happens even at low glucose. Because insulin is released regardless of meals, they can cause severe, unpredictable hypoglycaemia. They need functioning beta cells, so they do not work in type 1 diabetes.

cards.front: Why must insulin be injected, and what is its plasma half-life?
cards.back: Insulin is a peptide that is broken down in the gut, so it is ineffective orally. It is distributed only in extracellular fluid, and its plasma half-life is about 5 to 9 minutes. Nearly half of pancreatic insulin is cleared by the liver on first pass.

cards.front: What are the onset, peak and duration of regular insulin, and how should it be timed?
cards.back: KDT: onset 30 to 60 minutes, peak 2 to 3 hours, duration 6 to 8 hours (Katzung: effect within 30 min, peak about 2 h, lasts 5 to 7 h). Because absorption from the s.c. site is slow, it is optimally injected about 1 hour before a meal (KDT); injected just before eating it gives early post-meal hyperglycaemia and late hypoglycaemia. It is unsuitable for basal cover. Given IV its action is prompt, and it is the insulin used for IV infusion in DKA.

cards.front: Name the rapid-acting insulin analogues and how they are timed.
cards.back: Insulin lispro (B28 and B29 residues reversed), insulin aspart (B28 proline replaced by aspartate) and insulin glulisine. They act within about 15 minutes, peak at 1 to 2 hours and last 3 to 5 hours. Lispro is given 0 to 20 minutes before a meal, giving better meal-time control and fewer late hypoglycaemic episodes than regular insulin.

cards.front: What is insulin glargine, and how is it given?
cards.back: A long-acting analogue that forms a depot after injection and releases a steady, peakless level for up to 24 hours. It is given once daily, often at bedtime, for basal cover; it does not control meal-time glucose. It is acidic and cannot be mixed with other insulins. It causes fewer night-time hypoglycaemic episodes than NPH.

cards.front: How do DPP-4 inhibitors lower blood glucose?
cards.back: They block DPP-4, the enzyme that breaks down GLP-1 and GIP, so incretin levels rise. This increases glucose-dependent insulin release and reduces glucagon, so hypoglycaemia risk is low and the drugs are weight neutral. Vildagliptin and saxagliptin bind DPP-4 covalently; sitagliptin binds without a covalent bond. Adverse effects: nasopharyngitis and upper respiratory infection, hypersensitivity (angioedema, Stevens-Johnson syndrome), possible pancreatitis, joint pains; saxagliptin and alogliptin have been linked to heart failure.

cards.front: How do GLP-1 receptor agonists lower glucose, and what are their main adverse effects?
cards.back: Exenatide is based on exendin-4, a lizard peptide that DPP-4 does not degrade. Liraglutide is GLP-1 with a C16 fatty acid chain; albumin binding hinders DPP-4 access and slows absorption, giving a half-life of about 12 hours and once-daily dosing (GG14 calls it DPP-4 resistant). Semaglutide is resistant through a position-2 substitution and binds albumin tightly (half-life 7 days; weekly injection or daily oral form). All act on GLP-1 receptors: glucose-dependent insulin release, less glucagon, slower gastric emptying and less appetite, so weight falls. Adverse effects: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea; pancreatitis risk; avoid with medullary thyroid carcinoma (GLP-1 receptors on C cells).

cards.front: How do SGLT-2 inhibitors act, and what are their main safety concerns?
cards.back: They block SGLT2 in the proximal tubule, lowering the renal threshold for glucose and causing glycosuria. This lowers HbA1c by about 0.5 to 1%, with weight loss and little hypoglycaemia. They reduce heart failure hospitalisation and slow diabetic kidney disease, so they are used early in patients with cardiovascular disease, heart failure or nephropathy. Risks: genital mycotic and urinary infections, volume depletion and hypotension, ketoacidosis with near-normal glucose. Glucose-lowering efficacy falls with renal impairment: not recommended for glycaemic control below eGFR 45 and contraindicated below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2.

cards.front: How does pioglitazone work, and what limits its use?
cards.back: It is a PPAR-gamma agonist acting mainly in fat and muscle, where it enhances insulin-responsive gene expression and GLUT4 translocation. It improves insulin sensitivity without raising insulin levels, and it lowers triglycerides and raises HDL. Limitations: fluid retention, weight gain, heart failure, fractures and the need for liver monitoring. A possible bladder cancer link has been reported, though large studies disagree. It is contraindicated in heart failure and liver disease.

cards.front: How do you treat an episode of insulin-induced hypoglycaemia?
cards.back: Give 15 to 20 g of oral glucose or sugar, and repeat after 15 to 20 minutes if there is no improvement. In severe cases give 30 to 50 mL of 50 percent glucose IV over about 10 minutes. If the patient cannot take sugar and IV glucose is not available, glucagon 0.5 to 1 mg can be given as a stopgap; a 3 mg nasal glucagon device is now available. KDT also lists adrenaline 0.2 mg s.c. as a less desirable option. Continue oral carbohydrate because hypoglycaemia may recur.

cards.front: How is insulin given in diabetic ketoacidosis?
cards.back: Regular insulin IV only, alongside aggressive IV hydration (normal saline first) and potassium replacement. The usual starting infusion is about 0.1 U/kg/h; KDT precedes it with an IV bolus of 0.1 to 0.2 U/kg and doubles the rate if glucose has not fallen significantly in 2 hours (a fall of about 10% per hour is adequate). When glucose reaches about 300 mg/dL (usually in 4 to 6 h), KDT reduces the infusion to 2 to 3 U/h and adds 5% glucose, continuing until the patient is fully conscious and can start s.c. insulin.

The insulin used for IV infusion

Glargine: peakless, lasts about 24 hours, acidic, not mixed with other insulin

points: Diet and exercise come first; drugs add to them, not replace them
Target HbA1c below 7 percent
Metformin, unless contraindicated or not tolerated
Weight neutral, rarely causes hypoglycaemia
With cardiovascular disease, heart failure or nephropathy: SGLT2 inhibitors early (heart failure and kidney benefit); GLP-1 receptor agonists also have cardiovascular benefit
Where weight loss matters: GLP-1 receptor agonists or tirzepatide
Sulfonylureas: effective and cheap, but weight gain and hypoglycaemia, and lose efficacy over years
DPP-4 inhibitors: weight neutral, low hypoglycaemia, moderate HbA1c fall
Glinides for post-prandial hyperglycaemia

Acarbose as a mild adjunct, limited by flatulence
Many patients eventually need insulin

cards.front: Essay: insulin therapy in type 1 diabetes

points: Type 1 always requires insulin, as does diabetes after pancreatectomy
Regimen must provide basal suppression of hepatic glucose output plus meal-time coverage
Human insulin or insulin analogues (rapid, short, intermediate and long acting)
Split-mixed: two injections, poor lunch-time cover
Basal-bolus: three or four injections, most physiological

Continuous s.c. insulin infusion (pumps) uses short-acting insulins: basal rates plus programmed meal boluses; pumps linked to continuous glucose monitors are moving toward closed-loop automated delivery
Teplizumab (anti-CD3 antibody), a 14-day infusion in high-risk stage 2 individuals aged 8 and above, delays onset of clinical type 1 diabetes by about 2 years
Pre-filled syringes and pen devices
Inhaled insulin is not for smokers or COPD patients
Hypoglycaemia is the main danger
Local reactions and lipodystrophy; allergy is now rare
Oedema on starting; loss of warning symptoms with time

cards.front: Essay: acute metabolic emergencies in diabetes

points: Causes and symptoms, from autonomic to neuroglucopenic
Oral glucose, IV glucose, glucagon as a stopgap
Prevent recurrence by reviewing dose, meals and interacting drugs
Absent or inadequate insulin; ketosis, pH below 7.3 and low bicarbonate
Precipitants: new type 1 diabetes, missed insulin, infection, pancreatitis, high-dose steroids; euglycaemic DKA with SGLT2 inhibitors
Aggressive IV fluids starting with normal saline
IV regular insulin, about 0.1 U/kg/h, with frequent glucose monitoring
5 percent glucose added once glucose reaches about 300 mg/dL (KDT), because glucose falls before ketones clear
Maintain potassium and other electrolytes; bicarbonate only for severe acidosis
Glucose over 600 mg/dL and osmolality over 320 mOsm/L without acidosis, mostly in elderly type 2 patients
Aggressive rehydration; low-dose insulin; less potassium, alkali usually not needed
Prophylactic heparin because of thrombosis risk
Early, vigorous treatment of the metabolic state and the trigger
Mortality in hyperosmolar coma remains high

cards.front: Classify: oral antidiabetic drugs by class
cards.text: Biguanide: {{metformin}}. Sulfonylureas: {{glimepiride}}, {{gliclazide}}. Glinides: {{repaglinide}}, {{nateglinide}}. Thiazolidinedione: {{pioglitazone}}. Alpha-glucosidase inhibitor: {{acarbose}}.

GLP-1 agonists: {{exenatide}}, {{liraglutide}}, {{dulaglutide}}, {{lixisenatide}}, {{semaglutide}}. SGLT-2 inhibitors: {{canagliflozin}}, {{dapagliflozin}}, {{empagliflozin}}, {{ertugliflozin}}.

cards.front: Classify: insulins by duration of action
Classify: drugs that change sulfonylurea effect
Classify: antidiabetic choices in pregnancy
cards.text: {{Insulin}} is the drug of choice for diabetes in pregnancy. {{Metformin}} has been shown to be safe and effective in gestational diabetes, though it is not FDA-approved for it. {{Pioglitazone}} should not be used in pregnancy, and the safety of {{sulfonylureas}} is not established, so patients are switched to insulin.

cards.front: Tirzepatide: what is it, and how does it compare with GLP-1 agonists?
cards.back: A dual GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist, built on the GIP sequence with a fatty diacid chain that binds albumin, allowing once-weekly s.c. injection. Started at 2.5 mg weekly and raised in 2.5 mg steps every 4 weeks up to 15 mg. It lowered HbA1c by about 1.9 to 2.6% with weight loss of about 6 to 13 kg, and improved lipids, blood pressure and fatty liver. Safety resembles GLP-1 agonists: dose-related nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea, and a slightly higher pancreatitis rate.

cards.front: Teplizumab: mechanism and use?
cards.back: A humanised monoclonal antibody against CD3, the main signalling part of the T-cell receptor, which modulates the autoimmune attack on beta cells. It is given as a daily infusion for 14 days to people aged 8 and above at high risk of type 1 diabetes (two positive autoantibodies with impaired glucose tolerance, stage 2). It delays the onset of clinical (stage 3) type 1 diabetes by about 25 months. Adverse effects: transient fall in white cells and lymphocytes, rash, headache.

cards.front: Short note: GnRH analogues

points: Hypothalamic GnRH is released in pulses that stimulate FSH and LH
Continuous exposure desensitises pituitary gonadotropes and stops gonadotropin release
Goserelin, leuprolide, nafarelin and triptorelin are more potent and longer-acting than native GnRH
Initial stimulation is followed by receptor down-regulation, giving reversible chemical castration or oophorectomy
Uses: precocious puberty, prostate cancer (with an antiandrogen to cover the initial surge), endometriosis, premenopausal breast cancer, uterine fibroids and IVF pretreatment
Ganirelix and cetrorelix: short-acting, given daily, prevent the LH surge in controlled ovarian stimulation
Degarelix and abarelix: long-acting, used for androgen withdrawal in advanced prostate cancer
Menopausal symptoms: hot flushes, sweating, vaginal dryness, low libido
Osteoporosis risk if used for more than about 6 months
